chapter: Working with Duke and final reflections
title: 'Black, Brown and Beige', 'Come Sunday' and the Chicago show
summary: Whaley orchestrated 'Come Sunday' and 'Black, Brown and Beige' in Hollywood, and describes the 1963 Chicago show with Alvin Ailey and the rising pit.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: You know, I was in Los Angeles, Hollywood when we made 'Black, Brown & Beige,' and this thing was -- you know, it stuck in my mind -- da, da, da, da, That's a number that Johnny Hodges made famous.

But I orchestrated it for him, and all that show, and I asked Duke, what are you gonna do with this, and he didn't say nothing, see, and in '63 we went to Chicago and that's where he incorporated nearly all -- every tune that was in 'Black, Brown & Beige,' he put in the show. That was great, that was a great show out there.
Oh, I wish I had seen that.

Oh, that was a great show, and I said to Duke, this should go into the World's Fair, this show should be in the World's Fair because it depicted the negro in music from nothing up to lawyers, doctors, preachers and all politicians and everything. He had them all on the stage. Opened up with the -- down in the pit and they were all in rags and then the pit slowly rolls up and -- yeah. They
had this boy they're writing so much about --
No, down at the City Center, he's got this dance group. Anyway, this guy and a girl ...
Alvin Ailey, that's it. He had a girl -- tall, thin, black gal.

Yeah, and she and him were doing a dance, and they had just a spotlight on her -- everything was black but the spotlight on them, and they danced for about a minute or so and then the pit started rising and showed all these people. Oh, it was beautiful. I used to be copying and I'd run and go in the orchestra and sit down and listen to the music and want to listen to the music and listen to the people singing. Oh ...
